rv.q: He’s found a way to scramble enough of the structure of a boy-meets-girl romantic drama to thrill, if not leave a deep impression.
But there’s no denying that it packs a powerful punch.
White is deft at creating moods of mystery and confusion that convincingly mimic the experience of alcohol-induced memory loss.
The result is more irritating than cathartic.
The effect is initially fascinating, but ultimately exhausting — like enduring the slurry rant of that friend who’s had two too many and now just won’t shut up.
White—with skilled assistance from director Rory McGregor and a team of very good theatrical designers—gives this short, insightful drama a 21st-century sheen.
It’s a beguiling, heart-wrenching ninety-minute pas de deux as two lost souls try to find love and escape together.

This could have been a maudlin, heavy-handed treatise on the dangers of addiction, but Blackout Songs is surprisingly seductive, drawing the audience in with the charisma of its two leads even as it depicts how frightening, unmooring, and destructive alcohol dependence can be.
White’s acting showcase stands as a riveting piece of theatre that lingers long after the curtain call.
As these co-dependents, Lee and Teague give bravura performances which remain high-powered throughout.
The American premiere of this 2022. British drama features two blackout drunks who are as addicted to each other as they are to the bottle.
Like many a drunk, Blackout Songs isn't as captivating as it thinks it is.
Abbey Lee and Owen Teague hurl themselves into the outsize roles with a fearless abandon that is both impressive and numbingly one-note over the course of a very long 90 minutes
